_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 12 Rocks and Fossils. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in order (only one planet; out of the rocks; oil and gas; a fossil; taking carefully, with the lesson's fact-card step as its own chapter before it), in the lesson's own words and with its own pictures: its six explore items, its two sorting bins, its fossil demo (ART.scene fossil 0-3) and its four Earth-and-us cards.
title: Rocks and Fossils
subtitle: Grade 3 Science
objectives: Know that planet Earth is the source of all the materials we use and that many useful materials, including oil, natural gas and metals, come from or are found in rocks.
Know that fossils are impressions, or remains, of things that were once alive.
Use observations and tests to sort, group and classify objects.
Use secondary information sources to research an answer to a question.
Identify risks and explain how to stay safe during practical work.
Know that everyone uses science and identify people who use science professionally.
Talk about how science helps us understand our effect on the world around us.

beats.say: A metal spoon, a glass window, a bottle of petrol.
All three came out of rocks, deep in planet Earth.
Every material we use comes from planet Earth.
There is nowhere else. Not the Moon, not the Sun.
Wood and wool come from living things.
Metal, glass, oil and gas come from rocks.
So there are two sources: the rocks, and the living things on top.
Metal is found inside rocks called ores.
The rock is dug up and heated, and the metal is separated out.
That is where the metal in your spoon began.
Glass is melted sand, and sand is tiny bits of rock.
Bricks are baked clay. Clay is a soft rock.
Oil and natural gas are trapped deep in rocks underground.
The oil is pumped up to the surface.
Some of it is made into petrol, and cars burn it.
Some becomes plastic. So even a plastic bottle began in the Earth.
Millions of years ago, a fish swims in the sea.
It dies, and sinks into the soft mud at the bottom.
More mud settles on top, layer after layer.
The weight squashes the mud into rock, with the fish's shape pressed inside.
One day the rock splits open, and there is the fish.
Not the fish itself. Its shape, pressed in like a footprint. That is a fossil.
Where would you look for a fossil? You can look it up.
A fact card is a secondary source. Somebody found it out and wrote it down for you.
Fossils are found in rock made of layers of mud or sand, like sandstone.
Most are hard parts: shells, bones and teeth. A jellyfish rarely leaves one.
Look at cliffs and beaches. Go with a grown-up, and never stand under a cliff.
A quarry cuts rock out of a hillside, and leaves a huge hole.
A spill can cover beaches and birds in oil, so it is done very carefully.
Recycle a can, and less rock has to be dug up.
A geologist studies rocks. A palaeontologist studies fossils.
Science helps us see the harm, and do less of it.
Everything you use comes from planet Earth.
Metal from ore, glass from sand, oil from deep in the rock.
A fossil is the shape of something once alive, kept in rock.
Look it up, and recycle. Then less has to be dug up.
